fields.sample_size: Single-settlement case study of Kathputli Colony (Shadipur, Delhi; a legally notified slum; about 2,500 households in Kathputli Basti): on-site interviews and a questionnaire survey from March to July 2010 mentioned only in a note; no sample size, sampling or instruments are reported; context from Delhi Jal Board data (about 70% of the city's population covered, 55% of connections metered)
fields.effect_measure: qualitative case study organised by Swyngedouw's four strategies (passive acceptance, individual resistance, self-help, social mobilisation); no quantitative estimate
fields.effect_estimate: The strategies overlap and none produced structural change: water remains a 'claim', not a 'right'. In Kathputli Basti there is no drinking-water pipeline and the standposts are mostly dry; about 100 of 300 households in one lane get hard water for 3-4 hours a day from an MLA-funded borewell; the nearest tap is outside the colony (2-3 hours' queue in summer); vendors sell water at Rs 5 per litre can. In Bihari Basti residents illegally punctured a main and built a network with individual connections, and sell water to other pockets; the Delhi Jal Board stopped sending tankers after violence between residents and crews. The author argues that the State's power to legalise or make illegal settlements controls access, cites the 2002 Supreme Court reading of Article 21 as including the right to water, and notes that the Board's reform plans do not address the problem.
